URL: https://www.iranintl.com/en/202611246967
Iran International, 24 Nov 2026 08:37 GMT

The dollar traded at a record 2,830,000 rials, up around 6% from 2,642,000 on November 12. The euro climbed to 3,110,000 rials, while the British pound reached 3,730,000 rials.

The latest plunge in Iran’s currency came a day after Washington imposed sanctions on 22 entities and eight individuals involved in the Islamic Republic’s overseas financial networks.

“Iran’s economy is underwater, and its leaders are panicking,” US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said. “Iran’s shadow banking system is the last financial lifeline of a bankrupt regime.”

The measures targeted the Iran Center for Exchange of Currency and Gold, which facilitates tens of billions of dollars in annual trade by connecting exporters earning foreign currency with importers.

A separate Treasury report identified $14.7 billion in transactions potentially linked to Iranian shadow banking networks between January 2025 and August 2026.

Accelerating currency depreciation

The dollar now trades at more than 3.4 times its value in June 2025, when it stood at around 820,000 rials following the outbreak of the 12-day war.

The depreciation has coincided with Washington’s tightening naval blockade and efforts to restrict Iranian oil sales and disrupt the transfer of export revenues.

100%Bundles of Iranian rial and US dollar banknotes lie on the counter of a currency exchange shop.$RS("S:d","P:d")Several economists have warned in recent months of the risk of hyperinflation as Iran grapples with declining production, foreign currency shortages and mounting trade restrictions.

Iranian officials have meanwhile blamed currency market participants for exchange rate instability.

The weakening currency is driving up the cost of imported raw materials, medicines, medical equipment and consumer goods.

For Iranian households already struggling with stagnant or overdue wages and rising housing, food and healthcare costs, the dollar’s continued rise threatens to further erode purchasing power.

"])•••$RC("B:5","S:5")More StoriesFlogging of Iranian singer Parastoo Ahmadi sparks outrage on social mediaNov 24, 2026, 03:47 GMT+0Listen to this article100%Iranian singer Parastoo Ahmadi performs alongside her band at the historic Deir-e Gachin Caravanserai near Qom, Iran, in December 2024.The flogging of Iranian singer Parastoo Ahmadi and four members of her concert team on Monday sparked outrage on social media, with artists, activists and other users condemning the punishment and denouncing restrictions on women’s artistic expression in Iran.

Ahmadi, concert organizer Mohsen Lashkari and musicians Soheil Faghih-Nasiri, Amin Taheri and Amirali Pirnia each received 74 lashes at the prosecutor’s office in Qom, their lawyer Mostafa Nili said.

Women have been banned from singing solo in public in Iran since the 1979 Islamic Revolution.

Singer Mehdi Yarrahi, who himself received 74 lashes in March 2025 over a protest song challenging compulsory hijab, shared footage of Ahmadi’s performance on Instagram, expressing solidarity with her and her concert team.

Musician Hana Kamkar also condemned the punishment in an Instagram video, asking Islamic Republic officials what the artists had offered other than humanity, joy and beauty.

Ahmadi’s December 2024 concert was filmed at the historic Deir-e Gachin Caravanserai near Qom, a Shiite holy city and a center of religious conservatism in Iran.

Wearing a long, sleeveless black dress with her hair uncovered, Ahmadi sang alongside male musicians in a performance staged without a live audience. The virtual concert, which defied both mandatory hijab rules and restrictions on women singing publicly, has drawn more than 3.2 million views on YouTube.

Activist Zeinab Zaman highlighted the contrast between the virtual performance and the physical punishment inflicted on the singer.

“Her concert was virtual, but the lash on her body was real,” Zaman wrote on X. “We are recording act after act of courage and shame upon shame in this history. Bodies are eyewitnesses.”

The flogging also reignited accusations of double standards in the Islamic Republic’s treatment of female singers.

In April, as Iran was at war with the United States and Israel, footage of Lebanese singer Julia Boutros was screened at nighttime gatherings of government supporters in Tehran’s Ferdows Garden. Boutros is known for her songs in support of the Lebanese resistance.

Translator Emily Amraee recalled the gatherings in a post on X, noting that the authorities had “enthusiastically” broadcast the Lebanese singer’s performances over several consecutive nights, only to flog an Iranian woman for singing months later.

Others questioned the government’s priorities amid a conflict it has portrayed as a threat to its very existence.

“If possible, in the midst of what you yourselves call an ‘existential’ war, refrain from flogging the daughters of this country. Is that so difficult for you?” Mojtaba Najafi wrote on X.

Mahmood Amiry-Moghaddam, director of Norway-based Iran Human Rights, pointed to the government’s failure to address the country’s economic and infrastructure crises while continuing to punish women for defying its restrictions.

“She sang; the Islamic Republic responded with the lash,” he wrote on X.

“A government that is incapable of resolving the crises of livelihoods, water and electricity, yet does not hesitate to flog a woman for her voice, has reached the end of its life.”

The communications office of Iran’s exiled Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi condemned the flogging in a statement on X, describing it as an attempt to humiliate and suppress the artists and accusing the Islamic Republic of fearing women’s voices.

“The virtual concert staged by Parastoo Ahmadi, a young artist, two years ago and livestreamed on social media remains a lasting symbol of the voices of Iranian women who cannot be silenced,” the statement said.

“Before 1979, Iran was a cradle of art and music and women were pioneers in these fields. Today, however, the regime flogs courage and beauty,” it added.

The statement said the Islamic Republic would soon fall and that women would once again play a prominent role in Iran’s artistic, social, economic and political life.

Ahmadi and the four members of her concert team were convicted of offending public decency by producing and publishing what the court deemed vulgar and immoral content online.

An appeals court upheld their sentences in September, including two-year bans on artistic and musical activities and foreign travel.

Amnesty International had previously called on Iranian authorities to halt the flogging sentences, describing flogging as torture and urging an end to compulsory hijab and corporal punishment.

Listen to this article100%Iranian flags hang next to a missile on display during the forty-seventh anniversary of the Islamic Revolution in Tehran, Iran, February 11, 2026. Majid Asgaripour/WANA/ReutersAn Iranian lawmaker’s claim that Tehran’s missiles can now travel 4,500 kilometers and a front-page boast by Tehran daily Hamshahri that all of Europe is within reach have renewed questions about Iran’s ability to strike the continent.

Experts told Iran International the threat should be taken seriously, though Iran has yet to demonstrate that it can reliably hit targets at that distance.

Ahmad Bakhshayesh Ardestani, a member of Iran’s parliamentary National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, made the 4,500-kilometer claim on Monday without offering technical evidence.

Hamshahri, a newspaper run by Tehran’s municipality, touted a range of roughly 5,000 kilometers. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has said it lifted its self-imposed 2,000-kilometer limit but has given no details about whether longer-range missiles have been deployed.

100%What the Diego Garcia launches showed

The clearest indication that Iran may have exceeded its old 2,000-kilometer limit came in March, when it reportedly fired two missiles toward Diego Garcia, a joint US-British military base in the Indian Ocean. One was intercepted and the other failed in flight.

Jim Lamson, a senior research associate at the James Martin Center for Nonproliferation Studies at Middlebury College, assessed that both were intermediate-range ballistic missiles, or IRBMs, capable of traveling at least 4,000 kilometers.

“It does show that Iran had developed at least prototypes of IRBMs, but their design and production status remain unclear,” Lamson said.

He said US and Israeli strikes damaged Iran’s missile development and production facilities, leaving it unclear whether Tehran could build more of those missiles in the near term.
